summary: Describes how GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling can be extended to support Calls, which are associations between endpoints and key transit points that do not carry traffic themselves but let later connections be made. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Before building any roads, two towns first agree they will work together. Later, actual roads are built under that agreement.

questions: what is the difference between a call and a connection in gmpls
what is the c bit in admin_status
how are calls set up with rsvp-te
subtitle: How GMPLS signaling sets up an agreement between two endpoints before any actual connection is built.

tldr.problem: Some networks need an association between endpoints, and sometimes key transit points, to support a service. That association must exist apart from the label switched paths that carry the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Calls, set up with RSVP-TE Notify messages marked by a new C bit in the ADMIN_STATUS object. A 16-bit short Call ID in the SESSION object ties each LSP to its Call, and a long Call ID travels in the Session Name.
tldr.outcome: Calls and Connections are fully and logically separate. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3473 and is itself updated by RFC 6001.

today: RFC 4974 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3473. It is itself updated by RFC 6001, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Calls in GMPLS
sections.content:
A Call is an association between endpoints, and possibly between key transit points such as network boundaries, in support of an instance of a service. The end-to-end association is the Call. The association between two transit points, or between an endpoint and a transit point, is a Call Segment. An entity that processes either is a Call Manager.

A Call does not carry user traffic. It only builds a relationship by which later Connections can be made. In GMPLS a Connection is a Label Switched Path (LSP). A Call may have zero, one or many Connections, and a Connection belongs to zero or one Call.

RFC 4974 does not change the Connection setup procedures of RFC 3473. It is motivated by the ITU-T ASON architecture and the requirements in RFC 4139, but the RFC says it has wider applicability and works for packet, layer-2, TDM, lambda and fiber switching interfaces.
sections.eli5: A Call is a promise between two places that they will cooperate. It is not the road itself; roads, called connections, come later.

sections.title: Calls, Connections and Their IDs
sections.content:
Calls give you identification and verification of the initiator before LSP setup, support for virtual concatenation with diverse path LSPs, grouping of several LSPs under one Call, and help with control plane operations. A Call involves transit nodes only to forward Call management requests as transparent messages, while Connections need state along the data path.

The RFC requires full separation. It MUST be possible to set up a Connection without a Call, a Call without Connections, and several Connections under one Call. Removing the last Connection SHOULD NOT automatically remove the Call, except as local policy at the ingress. Signaling a Connection MUST NOT require Call state in the network.

The identifiers form a hierarchy. Call IDs are unique for a source and destination address pair, Tunnel IDs are unique within a Session, and LSP IDs are unique within a Tunnel. A Call_ID of zero is reserved and MUST NOT be used for Call establishment.

The RFC also describes using Call setup to exchange access link capabilities when routing protocols cannot supply them, for example at a user-to-network interface.
sections.eli5: Each agreement gets a name tag. Roads built under it carry the same tag, so anyone can tell which agreement a road belongs to. Zero means no agreement.

sections.title: New Fields and Objects
sections.content:
Calls use the RSVP Notify message, which is targeted and does not need to follow the path of LSPs. Setting up a Call and a Connection in one step (piggybacking) is not supported. The extensions are:

  • Long Call ID. A byte sequence, 40 bytes being called not unreasonable, carried in the Session Name field of the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object on the Call setup Notify. Core nodes MUST forward it transparently.
  • Short Call ID. A 16-bit Call_ID in the SESSION object, using a field that was previously reserved. It is zero when there is no Call, which keeps older nodes compatible. It MUST NOT be used to decide which session an RSVP message applies to.
  • LINK_CAPABILITY object. Class-Num 133, C-Type 1, optional on Call setup Notify messages, carrying subobjects that describe a link: type 1 (IPv4 address), 2 (IPv6 address), 4 (unnumbered link identifier), 64 (Maximum Reservable Bandwidth) and 65 (interface switching capability descriptor). Only the first object in a message is processed.
  • C bit. A new Call Management bit in ADMIN_STATUS, set when the message manages a Call.

The Notify message also gains SESSION_ATTRIBUTE and optional LINK_CAPABILITY in its notify session sequence.
sections.eli5: The long name is the full title of the agreement, used once when it is made. The short number is a quick nickname that every road carries afterward.

sections.title: Setting Up and Tearing Down Calls
sections.content:
A Call is set up before and independent of its LSPs. The initiator sends a Notify with the R bit (to make the egress respond) and the C bit set in ADMIN_STATUS. ERROR_SPEC carries Error Code zero ("Confirmation"), and Message IDs MUST be used. The SESSION object holds a non-zero Call_ID, the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE carries the long Call ID, and bandwidth values are zero. The receiver MAY perform authorization and policy. If it accepts, it reflects the request, replaces any LINK_CAPABILITY with its own, and sets only the C bit.

Once a Call exists, LSPs with the same Call_ID belong to it. A Call MUST NOT be imposed on an LSP that already exists, because that would change its Session identifier. Calls are symmetric, so either end may add LSPs. The C bit MUST NOT be set on LSP messages.

Deleting a Call uses a Notify with R, D and C bits on the request and D and C on the response. Removing the last LSP does not remove the Call. A teardown request for a Call that still has LSPs MUST be rejected with the error value "Connections Still Exist". Either end may tear down an empty Call.
sections.eli5: One town sends a letter asking to team up and the other writes back yes. To end it, they exchange letters again, and you cannot cancel while roads under the deal still exist.

sections.title: Failures, Collisions and Keeping Calls Alive
sections.content:
If no Message ID acknowledgement arrives after the configured retries, the initiator SHOULD declare the Call failed and send a teardown. A receiver can reject a Call for security, authorization or policy reasons using existing RSVP error codes, or reply with error codes 13 ("Unknown object class") or 14 ("Unknown object C-Type") if it cannot parse the message.

Because Calls are symmetric, both ends may start a Call with the same long Call ID at once. The node with the numerically greater source address discards the received request and waits; the one with the smaller address discards its own attempt and answers. A duplicate of an existing Call gets the "Duplicate Call" error. If two distinct Calls get the same short Call ID, the greater address returns "Call ID Contention" and the other picks a new short ID.

To keep a Call alive, the initiator and terminator SHOULD send periodic Notify messages, with a RECOMMENDED period of twice the shortest refresh period of any associated LSP, and no less than one minute when there are none. Missing refreshes have no specific meaning; whether to tear down LSPs is a local policy matter.
sections.eli5: If both towns write the same letter at once, the one with the bigger address number waits for the answer. Towns also say hello regularly so each knows the other is still there.

sections.title: Applicability and Legacy Nodes
sections.content:
In network-initiated Calls, link properties are usually known from the IGP, so LINK_CAPABILITY is not usually needed. In user-initiated Calls, edge link information may not be visible in the core, so it may be included. The first core node may even generate the long and short Call IDs when the user edge node supplies neither. Third-party External Call Managers can apply policy at points that are neither initiator nor terminator, using normal IP routing between them to form Call Segments.

Nodes that do not support Calls fail in safe ways. A node without RSVP or GMPLS support will not acknowledge, so the initiator retries and gives up. A GMPLS node without Call support may fail to parse SESSION_ATTRIBUTE and return a parse error. If a transit node zeroes the formerly reserved field, the Resv message returns with the Call ID set to zero, which tells the initiator that some node is blocking Call management. Explicit routes may avoid such nodes, or they may need upgrading.
sections.eli5: Old post offices that do not know about the new agreements simply ignore the letter. The sender notices there is no reply and gives up.

sections.title: Security of Call Setup
sections.content:
Call setup is vulnerable to spoofing and denial of service. Since it uses Notify messages, it can be protected with the INTEGRITY object from RFC 2205 and RFC 3473, and deployments where security matters SHOULD use it. Deployments MAY also use IPsec or RSVP cryptographic authentication.

The RFC says Calls could add an extra level of authentication and policy for LSPs, but that needs more work on security associations meeting RFC 4107. Using Calls for that purpose before a security solution is standardized is called inappropriate. Key exchange is a remote procedure rather than a single-hop one, and IKEv2 is particularly suggested in RFC 3473.
sections.eli5: Anyone could fake a letter asking for an agreement, so the letters can be sealed with a signature. The RFC says not to rely on Calls for strong checking until a proper security method is ready.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned a new RSVP object, LINK_CAPABILITY, with Class-Num 133 (form 10bbbbbb, so nodes that do not recognize it drop it silently) and C-Type 1, defined only for Notify messages. IANA also keeps a list of its subobjects.

A new RSVP Error Code, Call Management (32), was assigned with four error values. The C bit of the ADMIN_STATUS object was assigned bit number 28 in the "Administrative Status Information Flags" sub-registry.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new names and flags were written in an official list so everybody uses the same ones.
